units.title: Website first impressions drive broad business judgments

claim.text: The source asserts that visitors judge the entire business and every metric based on the website's first impression, so perceptions rise purely because of the first impression.
claim.quote: every metric, the perception is that it is higher. And it's purely because of the first impression that the website gives.

unknowns: No measurement method or sample details are stated for the perception claim.

units.title: Same-company before-and-after website comparison

claim.text: The source presents a before-and-after website for the same company, where the newer website was judged as stronger.
claim.quote: both of these websites are for the same company. And in fact, this is a before and after of a website that we built for them.

unknowns: The metrics tested, respondent count, and method are not described.

units.title: Self-built site owners cannot accurately judge first-impression impact

claim.text: The source warns that if you built your own website, you are too close to judge whether it creates a positive or negative first impression.
claim.quote: If you've built your own site, you're too close to it to be able to judge whether it's going to be having a positive impact on first impressions or a negative impact on first impressions.

args.text: You have built your own website.
args.quote: If you've built your own site, you're too close to it to be able to judge whether it's going to be having a positive impact on first impressions or a negative impact on first impressions.

claim.quote: So, as well as using the logos there, we also mention the companies in this above the fold section there.

units.title: Include company name and job role in testimonials

claim.text: The source says testimonials should include not only the company name but also the job role of the person giving the testimonial.
claim.quote: And the testimonials not only include the company name, but the job role of the person that gave the testimonial.

action.text: Include the company name and the job role of the person in each testimonial.
action.quote: And the testimonials not only include the company name, but the job role of the person that gave the testimonial.

units.title: Effective testimonials act as before-and-after proof

claim.text: The source characterizes effective testimonials as before-and-after testimonials that let prospects resonate with the before situation and desire the after result.
claim.quote: these are essentially they're essentially before and after testimonials really that's what we're looking at here.

units.title: Display awards and Google reviews as credibility shortcuts

claim.text: The source recommends using awards and Google reviews as a great source of credibility and an immediate shortcut to credibility.
claim.quote: So here we've got some awards. This is on the Exposure Ninja website. Some awards that we've won and also some reviews from Google. great source of credibility, immediate shortcut to credibility

claim.text: The source recommends putting case studies on service pages as well as the case study page, and also notes putting them on every single page of the site.
claim.quote: putting them on every single page of the site.

action.text: Put case studies on the service pages as well as the case study page, and place them across every page of the site.
action.quote: as well as putting the case studies on the case study page. We'll actually put case studies on the service pages as well.

args.text: You have a case study page, but it tends to be one of the least visited pages on the site.
args.quote: In fact, it tends to be one of the least visited pages on the site.

units.title: Case studies cannot be overused

claim.text: The source asserts that you really cannot overuse case studies because they are such a powerful tool to build credibility.
claim.quote: you really can't overuse case studies. They're such a powerful tool to build credibility.

unknowns: No audience fatigue threshold or placement limit is stated.

units.title: Hyperniche by describing the customer's problem

claim.text: The source says when testimonials are lacking, one alternative credibility method is nailing someone's problem through hyperniching.
claim.quote: The first way is through nailing someone's problem. Basically, hyperniching.

action.text: Describe the target customer's problem in so much detail that they feel immediately understood and credibility is built.
action.quote: we've described their problem in so much detail that we immediately build credibility.

args.text: You are a new business with few testimonials and little work with clients.
args.quote: Well, yeah, but we're a new business. We haven't really got many testimonials.

unknowns: How to identify the niche or the specific problem details is not described.

units.title: Palm reader credibility by describing the situation

claim.text: The source uses a palm reader example to show that describing someone's situation accurately creates immediate credibility without testimonials or case studies.
claim.quote: When he sits down with a palm reader and the palm reader says, "Oh, so you've had this, this, and this in your life." She immediately has credibility with him.

units.title: Use your background or story as alternative credibility

claim.text: The source says another form of alternative credibility is your background or your story.
claim.quote: The next form of alternate credibility is your background or your story.

action.text: Tell your background or story in a way that resonates with the target audience.
action.quote: by telling them my story, I'd resonated with them.

args.text: You lack testimonials or need alternative credibility.
args.quote: So what if you don't have testimonials?

unknowns: What parts of a background story to use are not specified.

units.title: Professional drummer story creates a bond with musicians

claim.text: The source describes how mentioning his past as a professional drummer caused musicians to approach him and feel a bond.
claim.quote: if I mentioned the fact that I was I used to be a professional drummer a certain group of people would come up and find me at the end of the talk and mention the fact that they had also been a professional musician

claim.text: The source asserts that you have to resonate with the target audience, and telling your story did that.
claim.quote: You have to resonate with the target audience.

Looks like a much more established company. Website A maybe, you know, very small business. They probably don't have an HR person. probably don't pay very well, that type of thing. And it doesn't really matter what question I ask about the business. The result is that website B is always stronger. The business is always stronger. The product's better. Now, the punchline here is that both of these websites are for the same company. And in fact, this is a before and after of a website that we built for them. So, we built this website. It probably cost £4,000. And all of those first impressions, all of those judgments came free with the new website, right? So immediately people think the product's better. They think the customer service is better. They think the staff are happier. They think the online reviews are better. They think the wait times and the call cues are shorter. Every metric, doesn't matter what you ask, every metric, the perception is that it is higher. And it's purely because of the first impression that the website gives. Isn't that interesting? Isn't doesn't that just show us how judgmental we all are on first impressions? And people get a bit funny about this. People get a bit offended by first impressions and judgments. And they'll say things like, "Yeah, but we shouldn't judge people on first impressions. We shouldn't judge people on their appearances. You know, that's not a nice thing to do." Well, it may not be nice, but from an evolutionary perspective, it's actually programmed into us. We're actually programmed to be judgmental about people. It's actually really efficient because on the whole, you can actually tell a lot about someone from how they look. So whilst we might not like the fact that people are judging our business on the first impression of our website, well until they have any other information about our business, they really have nothing else to go on. So why would they not judge our entire business, every aspect on the look and feel of our website? People also get, you know, you see Instagram quotes saying you don't judge a book by their cover and all this type of stuff. That is exactly what book covers are for. So, if your website looks like website A, you've got an issue because people are judging you negatively, right? And by the way, quick word of warning for those who've built their own websites. Unfortunately, you're not able to accurately judge whether your website looks like an A or a B. Unfortunately, that's just the way it is. If you've built your own site, you're too close to it to be able to judge whether it's going to be having a positive impact on first impressions or a negative impact on first impressions. So, what I would do instead is contact exposion ninja for a free website and marketing review which you can get from our website or go to a website like useresting.com or something like that so that you can get an impartial perspective on how good your website is. Okay. Um, next form of credibility. Here on this website, we can see logos of the organizations that this company has worked with. So, we can see NHS, Deote, Lafage, Apatito, BBC. When we started working with, and by the way, this is a website that we've built for them. When we started working with them, we noticed on their about us page that they'd worked with these great companies, but they weren't shouting about this. You had to dig around on their website to find that information. And we thought, this doesn't make any sense. People shouldn't have to dig around to find that information. That information should be front and center. Because think about it, there's loads of credibility for knowing that you've chosen the same company that the BBC chose chooses, right? They could choose anyone, but they made the same choice that you're making. That gives your business so much credibility. So, as well as using the logos there, we also mention the companies in this above the fold section there. We say for over 11 years now, we've been helping the likes of Deote, BBC, NHS, and the Professional Cricketers Association, blah blah blah. So, we're using those companies again. We're referencing them. And then further down on the page, we even have testimonials as well. And the testimonials not only include the company name, but the job role of the person that gave the testimonial. So, why? Well, because firstly, meaningful specifics. We're being very specific about the job role that that person has. But also, think about the before and after. If I'm an events director looking for an AV company, I can see here that another events director has said this was a great choice. Well, that's the before and after, isn't it? I'm resonating with the before situation. That events director said quite simply, the best AV company I've ever dealt with. Well, that's the after that I'm looking for. That's the result that I really want. So, that's going to be really powerful to me as a potential buyer. So testimonials really important and these are essentially they're essentially before and after testimonials really that's what we're looking at here. Okay, next example um logos and awards and reviews. So here we've got some awards. This is on the Exposure Ninja website. Some awards that we've won and also some reviews from Google. great source of credibility, immediate shortcut to credibility, and a good way of showing your target audience that you're really good at what you do. Another form that you can drop into there. Next, we're going to talk about the use of case studies. Now, most businesses have some form of case study, obviously particularly relevant for service businesses, but a lot of businesses will have some form of case study. And how they usually use case studies is they will put them on a case studies page on their website. And that's great. You want to do that absolutely. But the downside with doing that is that not everybody visits the case study page on the website. In fact, it tends to be one of the least visited pages on the site. So, what we do when we're building a website is as well as putting the case studies on the case study page. We'll actually put case studies on the service pages as well. So, here you can see on the service page, we've shown some case studies. We've got the logos of the businesses as well. And these are case studies about this specific service that they offer. So, two things here. Firstly, people can read a case study if they want to find out more about the service, but secondly, they don't even need to. We know that people aren't necessarily going to click through and read the full case study, but they don't need to for us to get the benefit of that credibility because just by seeing the logo and knowing that that business has worked with us on this particular thing gives us that credibility, doesn't it? So, it's a great way of manufacturing and and kind of making the most of credibility and putting them on every single page of the site. So, you really can't overuse case studies. They're such a powerful tool to build credibility. So the question that we'll often get at this stage is, "Well, yeah, but we're a new business. We haven't really got many testimonials. We haven't done much work with people yet. So what if you don't have testimonials?" Well, the good news is there's a few different ways of picking up what we'd call alternative credibility. The first way is through nailing someone's problem. Basically, hyperniching. Let's say for example that you're an accountancy firm and you really want to work with uh technology startups at the early stage that are looking for investment. Okay. So let's say that on your website you said something like we work with early stage tech startups to um help them improve their numbers so that they can secure investment. Now, we've worked with uh we've worked with various different investors before and we know exactly what they're looking for. So, we can help you um develop this and we can help you put your numbers together so that you can get the investment that you're looking for and so that you can grow your business. Now, what we've just done there is we've completely nailed exactly what our customer is after. we've given them, we've described their problem in so much detail that we immediately build credibility. So my friend Big Chris, he goes to like palm readers and stuff like that. When he sits down with a palm reader and the palm reader says, "Oh, so you've had this, this, and this in your life." She immediately has credibility with him. She doesn't have to get the testimonials out. She doesn't have to read case studies because she's described his situation so accurately. It's almost like it hits you. You're like, "Oh, oh, wow. Okay." Yeah, no, you really understand my situation. So, it's a brilliant way of building credibility with an audience. The next form of alternate credibility is your background or your story. Now I noticed a while ago when I was giving a seminar if I mentioned the fact that I was I used to be a professional drummer a certain group of people would come up and find me at the end of the talk and mention the fact that they had also been a professional musician or they'd been a keen musician or they'd been a drummer. And I used to get confused by this, but then I realized that actually because they recognized an element of my story that produced a bond that made them feel like actually we were close because they were like, "Oh yeah, you're just like me." And it goes back to this thing about the before and after, doesn't it? You have to resonate with the target audience. And by telling them my story, I'd resonated with them.
